title: Trump: New York files a fraud lawsuit against Trump University
description_medium: In 2013, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman sued Donald Trump, Trump University, and a former university president, alleging persistent fraud and deceptive business practices. The state said the program misrepresented its instruction and instructors and sought $40 million. Those were allegations in a civil case, not criminal charges or a finding that Trump committed fraud.
description_long: In 2013, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman brought a civil lawsuit involving Trump University, Donald Trump, and the venture’s former president. The complaint alleged that the business used false and deceptive claims to sell real-estate seminars, including claims about instruction by Trump-selected experts and the program’s ability to help students succeed. The attorney general said the investigation covered consumer complaints from 2005 through 2011 and sought $40 million in restitution and penalties. Trump’s lawyer disputed the accusations and said the lawsuit contained falsehoods. The filing therefore began a contested civil case; it did not itself establish fraud or amount to a criminal prosecution. title: Trump Foundation made an illegal $25,000 contribution linked to Pam Bondi
description_medium: In 2013, the Trump Foundation made a $25,000 payment to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi while her office was considering complaints about Trump University. The foundation later corrected its tax filing and paid a $2,500 penalty. The Washington Post reported that the foundation acknowledged an illegal political contribution; the timing does not by itself establish a bribe or an exchange for official action.
description_long: The Donald J. Trump Foundation paid $25,000 in 2013 to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi, according to a 2016 Washington Post report. At the time, Bondi’s office was considering complaints concerning Trump University; her office later did not pursue the matter. The foundation had initially reported the payment as a donation to a Kansas charity with a similar name, though that charity did not receive the money. After the error was raised, the foundation corrected its tax filing and paid a $2,500 penalty. A Trump Organization official said the foundation reimbursed itself, and the foundation acknowledged the payment was an illegal political contribution. The documented facts establish a prohibited contribution and its timing alongside the office’s review. They do not establish that Trump paid Bondi personally, that Bondi agreed to exchange official action for the payment, or that the contribution caused her office’s decision. Calling it a bribe asserts a quid pro quo that the cited reporting does not prove; a precise account should describe the illegal political contribution and its consequences.

title: Supreme Court allows Hobby Lobby companies to claim a religious exemption under RFRA
description_medium: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. (2014), the Supreme Court held that closely held for-profit corporations could claim protection under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act against the federal contraceptive-coverage rule at issue. The ruling addressed a specific statutory dispute. It did not give corporations every right held by individuals, as the timeline headline suggests.
description_long: On June 30, 2014, the Supreme Court decided Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., a challenge to the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage requirement. The Court held that the closely held for-profit companies before it could invoke the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), and that applying the requirement to them violated that statute. The decision concerned the companies’ religious objections and the federal government’s chosen means of providing coverage; it did not declare that corporations possess every constitutional or human right held by individuals. The timeline’s claim that the Court ruled corporations have “human rights” broadly overstates the holding. The more precise account is that the Court interpreted RFRA to cover the closely held corporations in this case and found the particular mandate as applied to them unlawful under that act. The majority’s decision drew a dissent, but the core holding was limited to the statutory claim before the Court. This description relies on the published opinion text; the linked timeline page itself returned only site boilerplate.
